notes.title: Kestrel Health — contract and performance
notes.content:
Current agreement runs to December. Their denial rate against our book sits above the network average, driven mostly by one edit rule on a common medical-surgical code.

Their revenue cycle manager has raised it twice at claims level. He is not wrong that the rule is applied more tightly here than elsewhere, and that is a contract conversation neither of us has formally opened.

notes.title: Edit rule KR-114 — published position
notes.content:
The rule requires documentation of medical necessity for the code in question when billed with a specific modifier. It is published, it applies network-wide, and it has been in place two years.

That is the whole of what I can say about it. Why it was adopted, and how tightly it is applied elsewhere, is internal.

notes.title: What providers ask that I cannot answer
notes.content: Whether other providers get the same treatment. Every provider asks, every one of them is entitled to their own terms and nobody else's, and the question is always really about leverage.

notes.title: Appeals — Kestrel
notes.content: Forty of their appeals sit past our stated response window. That is our failure, not theirs, and it is a staffing problem on my side that I have not solved.

notes.title: Contract cycle
notes.content: Renewal discussions open ninety days before expiry. Rate proposals go through underwriting and are not mine to commit.

notes.title: Network portfolio
notes.content:
Eleven provider contracts in this region. Three hospital systems, the rest physician groups.

Contract cycles are staggered deliberately so that renewals do not all land in one quarter, which was somebody's good decision before my time.

notes.title: Rate setting — how it actually works
notes.content:
Underwriting sets the range from cost trend, utilisation, and the competitive position. I negotiate within it.

Providers assume I can move the number. I cannot, and saying so plainly early saves everyone a month.

notes.title: Edit rules — the standing argument
notes.content:
Every provider believes our edit rules are applied more tightly to them. Most are wrong. Occasionally one is right, and telling the difference requires looking rather than assuming.

When a provider brings data rather than a complaint, I look.

notes.title: Prior authorisation — our side of it
notes.content:
We know it is a burden. It also stops a measurable volume of low-value care.

Both are true. Public discussion of this never holds both at once and neither does most internal discussion.

notes.title: Appeals backlog
notes.content:
Running past our stated response window on a chunk of the queue. That is our failure.

Staffing. Two vacancies unfilled for four months in a role that is hard to hire for and easy to burn out in.

notes.title: Network adequacy
notes.content:
Regulatory requirement to have enough providers within distance and time standards.

Two specialties are thin in the rural part of the region. That constrains what I can push in a negotiation with the providers who cover them, and they know it.

notes.title: Value-based arrangements
notes.content:
Three contracts with quality-linked components. Attribution is the hard part — deciding which patients count toward whose performance.

Every dispute in these contracts is an attribution dispute wearing a quality argument.

notes.title: Provider relations — what makes it work
notes.content:
Answering the phone, doing what you said, and telling people no early rather than late.

Most of the friction in this job is created by slow no rather than by the no itself.

notes.title: Claims editing software
notes.content:
Third-party rules engine with our own overlay. The overlay is where local policy lives and where most disputes originate.

The overlay has grown by accretion and nobody has reviewed it end to end in three years.

notes.title: Medical policy updates
notes.content:
Published quarterly with sixty days notice. Providers say they do not see them.

They are emailed, posted, and in the portal, and providers still do not see them, which means the channel is wrong rather than the providers.

notes.title: What I cannot discuss
notes.content:
Another provider's rates, terms, or performance. Asked at least monthly, always for leverage.

The refusal is easy. The awkward part is that both sides know exactly why the question was asked.

notes.title: Prior authorisation — the volume conversation
notes.content: Providers say we require too many. We say the requirements target low-value care. Both positions have evidence and neither side has moved in three years.

notes.title: Provider relations — what the job actually is
notes.content: Mostly explaining a policy someone else wrote to someone who is losing money because of it, and identifying the small subset where they are right and I can do something.

notes.title: Claims edits — how one gets adopted
notes.content: Clinical evidence, an internal review, and a published notice. Once adopted it applies network-wide. Individual providers cannot have an exception, which is the first thing every provider asks for.

notes.title: Why I cannot discuss other providers' terms
notes.content: Every provider is entitled to their own terms and nobody else's. The question is always really about leverage and the answer is always the same.

notes.title: Escalation path
notes.content: Claims issues go to claims. Contract issues go to me. A contract issue raised as a claims issue circles for months, which is what is happening with one health system right now.

todos.title: Open the KR-114 conversation at contract level
todos.content: He is right that it belongs there. Two claims-level conversations were the wrong forum.
